cues.en: Sometimes the simplest questions have the most amazing answers.
cues.zh: 有时候，最简单的问题往往有着最惊艳的答案。

cues.en: Like, how can trees be so tall?
cues.zh: 比如，树为什么能长得这么高？

cues.en: It's a question that doesn't even seem like it needs an answer. Trees just are tall. Some of them are over a 100 meters. Why should there be a height limit? I'll tell you why.
cues.zh: 这个问题甚至看似不需要解答。树本来就很高，有的甚至超过100米。为什么会有高度限制呢？我来告诉你原因。

cues.en: Trees need to transport water from their roots up into their top most branches in order to survive, and that is no trivial task. There is a limit to the height that water can be sucked up a tube. It's 10 meters.
cues.zh: 树木为了生存，必须把水分从根部运送到最顶端的枝条，这绝非易事。用水管抽水其实是有高度极限的，只有10米。

cues.en: If you suck on a long vertical straw, the water will go no higher than 10 meters. At this point, there will be a perfect vacuum at the top of the straw and the water will start to boil spontaneously.
cues.zh: 如果你用一根很长的垂直吸管抽水，水面最高只能上升10米。此时，吸管顶端会形成绝对真空，水也会开始自发沸腾。

cues.en: For a tree to raise water a 100 meters, it would have to create a pressure difference of 10 atmospheres.
cues.zh: 树木要想把水提升100米，就必须产生10个大气压的压强差。

cues.en: How would trees do that? When I posed this conundrum, a lot of people said the answer is transpiration
cues.zh: 树木究竟是怎么做到的？当我抛出这个难题时，很多人说答案是蒸腾作用，

cues.en: and that's when water evaporates from the leaf pulling up the water molecules behind it. Now that's clearly a mechanism a tree can use to create suction but it doesn't help us overcome this 10 meter limit. The lowest the pressure can go is a pure vacuum which I imagine is not happening inside of tree leaks.
cues.zh: 也就是水分从叶片蒸发，拉动后面的水分子上升。这确实是树木产生吸力的一种机制，但它依然无法突破10米的极限。压强再低也不过是绝对真空，而且我认为树木内部显然不可能达到绝对真空。

cues.en: Right?
cues.zh: 对吧？

cues.en: Right, Hank. So you might suspect that a tree does not contain continuous straw like tubes. The tree effectively has valves in it, so you don't have a column of water. This big tube, which you're saying needs to be filled with water,
cues.zh: 没错，Hank。所以你可能会猜测，树木体内并没有像吸管那样连续相通的管道。树木实际上自带阀门结构，因此并不存在一整根连续的水柱。你说的这根需要充满水的大管子，

cues.en: is actually made up of cells.
cues.zh: 其实是由一个个细胞组成的。

cues.en: Although these are good speculations,
cues.zh: 虽然这些都是不错的推测，

cues.en: they don't turn out to be correct. Scientists who study trees find that the xylem tubes that transport water do contain a continuous water column. So how else could the tree transport water from the roots to the leaves? They don't suck. They don't use a vacuum. Okay.
cues.zh: 但它们并不正确。研究树木的科学家发现，负责输送水分的木质部导管中确实存在连续的水柱。那么树木还能怎样把水从根部运到叶片呢？它们不会吸。它们不用真空。好吧。

cues.en: So how do they do it? Squeezing like a cow, like you're squeezing a cow under all the way up. There's little tree muscles in there. Yeah. Besides being a giant waste of energy, all of the cells that make up the xylem tubes are dead.
cues.zh: 那它们是怎么做到的呢？像挤牛奶一样往上挤，一路挤上去。里面有小树肌肉。对。且不说这会极大浪费能量，构成木质部导管的所有细胞都是死的。

cues.en: What about osmotic pressure? If there is more solute in the roots than in the surrounding soil, water would be pushed up the tree. But some trees live in mangroves where the water is so salty that osmotic pressure actually acts in the other direction, so the tree needs additional pressure to suck water into the tree.
cues.zh: 那渗透压呢？如果根部的溶质浓度高于周围土壤，水就会被推上树。但有些树生长在红树林里，那里的水太咸，渗透压实际上方向相反，所以树需要额外的压力才能把水吸进树里。

cues.en: Then it must be capillary action.
cues.zh: 那就只能是毛细作用了。

cues.en: The thinner the tube, the higher the water can climb,
cues.zh: 管子越细，水能爬升得越高，

cues.en: but the tubes in a tree are too wide. At 20 to 200 micrometers in diameter, water should rise less than a meter. So how do trees do it?
cues.zh: 但树里的管子太宽了。直径在20到200微米之间，水应该上升不到一米。那树是怎么做到的？

cues.en: Well, one of the assumptions we made is wrong. The lowest the pressure can go is if you're vacuum. If you're vacuum. If vacuum. In a gas, this is true. When you eliminate all of the gas molecules, the pressure is zero and you have a perfect vacuum.
cues.zh: 嗯，我们做的一个假设是错的。压力最低只能到真空。如果你处于真空。如果真空。在气体中，这是对的。当你排除所有气体分子，压力为零，你就有了完美真空。

cues.en: But in a liquid, you can go lower than zero pressure and actually get negative pressures.
cues.zh: 但在液体中，压力可以低于零，实际上会形成负压。

cues.en: In a solid, we would think of this as tension.
cues.zh: 在固体中，我们会把这视为张力。

cues.en: This means that the molecules are pulling on each other and their surroundings.
cues.zh: 这意味着分子在相互拉扯，也在拉扯周围的环境。

cues.en: As the water evaporates from the pores of the cell wall, they create immense negative pressures of minus 15 atmospheres in an average tree. Think about the air water interface at the pore. There is one atmosphere of pressure pushing in and negative 15 atmospheres of suction on the other side. So why doesn't the meniscus break?
cues.zh: 随着水分从细胞壁的孔隙中蒸发，它们在普通树木中产生负15个大气压的巨大负压。想想孔隙处的气水界面。一侧有1个大气压的压力压入，另一侧有负15个大气压的吸力。那么，为什么弯月面不会破裂？

cues.en: Because the pores are tiny,
cues.zh: 因为孔隙很小，

cues.en: only two to five nanometers in diameter.
cues.zh: 直径只有2到5纳米。

cues.en: At this scale, water's high surface tension ensures the air water boundary can withstand huge pressures without caving.
cues.zh: 在这个尺度上，水的高表面张力确保气水边界能够承受巨大压力而不塌陷。

cues.en: As you move down the tree, the pressure increases up to atmospheric at the roots.
cues.zh: 当你沿着树向下移动时，压力会升高，到根部时达到大气压。

cues.en: So you can have a large pressure difference between the top and the bottom of the tree because the pressure at the top is so negative.
cues.zh: 所以树顶和树底之间可以存在很大的压力差，因为树顶的压力非常负。

cues.en: But hang on, if the pressure at the top is negative 15 atmospheres,
cues.zh: 但等等，如果树顶的压力是负15个大气压，

cues.en: shouldn't the water be boiling?
cues.zh: 水不应该沸腾吗？

cues.en: Yes.
cues.zh: 是的。

cues.en: Yes, it should.
cues.zh: 是的，应该沸腾。

cues.en: But changing phase from liquid to gas requires activation energy and that can come in the form of a nucleation site like a tiny air bubble. That's why it's so important that the xylem tubes contain no air bubbles and they can do this because unlike a straw, they've been water filled from the start.
cues.zh: 但从液态变为气态需要活化能，而这可以来自成核位点，比如一个微小的气泡。这就是为什么木质部导管中不能含有气泡如此重要，而它们能做到这一点，是因为与吸管不同，它们从一开始就充满了水。

cues.en: This way, water remains in the metastable liquid state when it really should be boiling. It's just like super cooled water remains liquid even though it should be ice. So you could say that the water in a tree is super sucked because it remains liquid at such negative pressures.
cues.zh: 这样一来，水就能维持在亚稳态的液态，而不是按理说应该沸腾。就像过冷水即使按理说应该结冰，也仍然保持液态一样。所以可以说，树里的水处于超强负压状态，因为它在如此低的压力下仍然是液体。

cues.en: And why are trees moving all this water up the tree? I want you to make a guess. Say it out loud. Photosynthesis?
cues.zh: 那树为什么要把这么多水一路往上输送呢？我想让你猜猜看，大声说出来。光合作用？

cues.en: Actually, no. Less than 1% of the water is used in photosynthetic reactions.
cues.zh: 其实不是。不到 1% 的水用于光合作用反应。

cues.en: Any other ideas? Okay. What about growth?
cues.zh: 还有别的想法吗？好，生长呢？

cues.en: Well, 5% of the water is used to make new cells. Well, so what happens to the other 95% of the water? It just
cues.zh: 嗯，5% 的水用于制造新细胞。那么剩下 95% 的水去了哪里？它只是

cues.en: evaporates.
cues.zh: 蒸发了。

cues.en: For each molecule of carbon dioxide a tree takes in, it loses hundreds of molecules of water. Woah. Can you believe how amazing this is? Trees create huge negative pressures of tens of atmospheres by evaporating water through nanoscale pores sucking water up a 100 meters in a state where it should be boiling but can't because the perfect xylem tubes contain no air bubbles just so that most of it can evaporate in the process of absorbing a couple molecules of carbon dioxide.
cues.zh: 树每吸收一个二氧化碳分子，就会失去数百个水分子。哇，你能相信这有多惊人吗？树通过纳米级孔隙蒸发水分，产生几十个大气压的巨大负压，把水吸上 100 米高。在这种状态下，水本该沸腾，却因为完美的木质部导管里没有气泡而没有沸腾，就这样，大部分水在吸收几个二氧化碳分子的过程中蒸发掉了。

cues.zh: 我以后再也无法用同样的眼光看树了。

cues.zh: 它们什么都不吃。这怎么说得通？我的意思是，
